case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 30-7-69 passed by the Dacca High Court in S. A. No. 827 of 1965).
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the Dacca High Court, setting aside in a Second Appeal a concurrent judgment of the Courts below and decreeing the suit brought by the respondents against the appellants for recovery of khas possession of the land in suit on declaration of their title thereto.

2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the land in suit comprises a plot of land being C. S Plot No.310 measuring '80 acre, which was recorded, along with CS. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre, as Koljote of one Mainuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of Defendants No.2 to 9, in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh P.S. Tejgaon, under the Jote of one Mani Mohan Dutta, which was recorded in Khatian No.82 of the mouza under the superior interest of one Haladhar Dey Sarkar. The father's name of Mainuddin was wrongly mentioned to be Ainuddin in Khatian No.83 in place of his correct name of Amir. The jote of Mani Mohan Dutta was put to auction in execution of a decree for arrears of rent obtained by Haladhar Dey Sarker and purchased by the decree-holder on 6-7-38. The sale was confirmed on 11-8-38 and delivery of possession of the auction purchased property was taken through Court on 23-1-39. The decree-holder auction purchaser having possessed the land for sometime settled the land of C S Plot No.311, on which the homestead was situated, with Mainuddin, son of Amir, at an annual rent of Rs. 1/6/-annas on the basis of a Kabuliyat executed on 27-3-39 and registered on 1-4-39. The other plot, namely C S. Plot No.310, remained in the khas possession of the auction-purchaser till 15-1-41, when the same was settled with the predecessor of plaintiffs No.1 to 18, and plaintiff No.19 off behalf of himself and on behalf of plaintiff No.20, on the basis of a registered Kabuliyat of the said date. Taking advantage of the wrong recording of the father's name of Mainuddin in the record-of-right defendant No.10 who happened to be an Advocate of the Dacca High Court, along with his relative defendant No.11, created some Kabalas in collusion with the heirs of Mainuddin to grab a portion of the land which has become valuable in the meantime. A dispute having arisen as to the possession of the land, defendant No.3, initiated a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in which possession having been found by the Magistrate, who was trying proceeding, in favour of the defendants, possession has been taken by the defendants from the receiver who had been appointed by the said Magistrate in the said proceeding.

3. Two sets of written statement were filed in this case, one by Defendants No.1 to 9 and the other by Defendants No.10 and 11 and the contentions raised therein are more or less the same. According to the contesting defendants, Mainuddin was a holder of an occupancy raiyati-right and was recorded as such in C.S. Khatian No.83 and his father's name also was correctly recorded therein as Ainuddin. The alleged auction sale of the interest of Mani Mohan Dutta, the landlord of Mainuddin is not true and, even if there had been any such auction-sale it did not affect the interest of Mainuddin, as it was a protected interest under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In case, however, such an interest is held to be an encumbrance it had not been annulled by service of a notice, as required under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The story of granting settlement by the alleged auction purchaser of C.S. Plot No.311 to Mainuddin or of C.S. Plot No.310 to the plaintiffs is without any foundation and Mainuddin and his heirs, during the old age of Mainuddin, and after his death, during the minority of Defendants No.2 and 3, had all along been in possession of the disputed land through the plaintiffs and their predecessors as bargadars.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit on holding on a consideration of the evidence on record and facts and circumstances of the case, that the plaintiffs had no right title and interest in the disputed land. In course of coming to the said decision it was held that the interest of Mainuddin was an occupancy raiyati right, which was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and that even if it was not a protected interest but was merely an encumbrance, the auction purchaser could not get khas possession of the land comprised in the tenancy of Mainuddin without annulling the said incumbrance. Although the defence case that the name of Mainuddin's father was Ainuddin was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge and the father's name, as given in the Kabuliyat, Ext.3 was found to be corrects the said Kabuliyat was disbelieved as not a genuine transaction. The learned Subordinate Judge also could not place any reliance upon the Dakhalias, Ext.4 series, produced in support of the plaintiff's claim of settlement, and negatived the plea of such settlement. On the question of possession, the learned Subordinate Judge was of the opinion that although the direct evidence of barga settlement of the suit land as set up by the defence, was not satisfactory but in the facts and circumstances of the case he was not in a position to reject the defence case on this count and on an analysis of the oral evidence, adduced by both the parties, came to the finding that the plaintiffs bargadar ploughed the land for 6/7 years after the death of Mainuddin and that the sons of Mainuddin began to possess the suit land one and a half years or so after the independence of the country.

5. The learned Additional District Judge who heard the appeal dismissed the same affirming all the findings of the trial Court The definite findings of the lower appellate Court were that the status of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat and as such was protected under section 160 of Bengal Tenancy Act, that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the Kabuliyat. Ext. 3, was executed by Mainuddin with full knowledge of its contents or that it was acted upon by Mainuddin by paying rent and that the Dakhilas, Ext.4 series, had been fabricated to bolster up the plaintiff's case.

6. The plaintiffs having preferred a Second Appeal against the aforesaid judgment to the Dacca High Court, a Division Bench of the said Court reversed the concurrent decision of the Court below and decreed the suit. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to have come to any positive finding on the question of the plaintiff’s title to the disputed land on the basis of the settlement alleged to have been granted by the decree-holder auction-purchaser, as pleaded in the plaint, but seem to have rested their decision in the appeal on the finding that the fight, title and interest of the defendants, if any, had been distinguished by the adverse possession of the plaintiffs, which does not appear to have been pleaded by the plaintiffs at any stage. The trial Court and the Court of first appeal positively negatived the plea of the settlement by disbelieving the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series, and holding them to be fabricated documents. The learned Judges of the High Court, however, expressed their view that the learned Additional District Judge misplaced the onus of proof as to the genuineness of the Dakhilas, Exts. 4 series on the plaintiffs aid was not justified in holding that no reliance could be placed on the said rent receipts.

7. On the basis of the entries in the records of right and other evidence on record the trial Court and the lower appellate Court came to the finding that the interest of Mainuddin was that of occupancy raiyat, which was a protected interest under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and as such had not been determined by the auction sale of the superior interest in the said disputed land and therefore the title of Mainuddin and that of his heirs after his death had remained unaffected by the said auction sale with the result that the plaintiffs could not acquire any interest by the alleged subsequent settlement granted to the plaintiffs even if it was true. The learned Judges of the High Court were of course of the opinion that the view of the Courts below that Mainuddin's interest was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was wrong and that in view of the admitted case that the plaintiffs had got into the possession of the disputed land it was not necessary to consider the defendant's alternative case as to the said interest being an encumbrance.

8. The learned Judges of the High Court have also been of the view that when Defendants No.1-9 disclaimed any concern with Mainuddin, son of Amir, but claimed themselves to be the successors of Mainuddin, son of Aminuddin the Courts below ought to have held that they had no locus standi to claim any interest in the suit land and the learned Additional District Judge having come to the finding that the defendants failed to prove barga settlement as well as surrender of the land by plaintiffs to the defendants after their barga settlement had been over and the said findings being contradictory with the later finding that the plaintiffs having entered into possession as bargadars under Mainuddin and his heirs, no question of limitation arose, the later finding was not acceptable and as such the right, title and interest of the defendants if any had been extinguished by the advance possession of the plaintiffs.

9. Special leave to appeal was granted by the Supreme Court of Pakistan on the question as to whether, having regard to the provision of section 48(g)(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the interest of Mainuddin was a protected interest under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and as to whether, in case the said interest was not found to be protected under section 160 of the Act it was, in any event, an encumbrance and was as such, annulled in accordance with the provision of section 167 of the said Act, even though this question of encumbrance and its annulment was not considered by any of the Courts below.

10. On reading the judgment of the learned Judges of the High Court and hearing the learned Counsel appearing for both the parties it appears however, that the said judgment also raises the question whether the learned Judges did properly reverse, in exercise of their powers under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below on the question of plaintiff's title and possession. We have allowed learned Counsel appearing for the parties to address the Court on this question as well.

11. At the outset it may be pointed out that the view of the learned Judges of the High Court that the defendants had no locus standi to claim any interest in the suit land in the context of their allegation as to the father's name of Mainuddin being Ainuddin was misconceived. The father's name of Mainuddin was found to be Amir and not Ainuddin as wrongly stated in the C.S. Khatian No.83. The case of the plaintiffs in this regard was accepted and that of the defendant's was rejected, by the said courts. It was the plaintiff's case that defendants No.1-9 was successors-in-interest of Mainuddin who was the holder of the land recorded in Khatian No.83. The defence case on this question was also the same. The difference between the two cases was only in respect of the father's name of Mainuddin. According to the plaintiff, it was Amir, as was mentioned in the Kabuliyat Ext.3, and not Ainuddin as was mentioned in the Khatian Ext. 6, but according to the defence, it was Ainuddin and not Amir and it has been correctly stated in the Khatian Ext.6. The learned Judges of the High Court have observed that as defendants No.1-9 had admittedly no connection with Mainuddin, son of Amir, the Courts below ought to have held that these defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land. It is not the case of the plaintiffs nor of the defendants that there were two Mainuddin, one being the son of Ainuddin and the other being the son of Amir and that the disputed land belonged either to Mainuddin son of Ainuddin or Maiauddin son of Amir. The findings of both the Courts below on this question were also that the defendants were the successors of Mainuddin, who was admittedly the holder of the land of Khatian No.83, but the father's name of the said Mainuddin was not Ainuddin, as claimed by the defendants, but was Amir, as asserted by the plaintiffs; So the observation of the learned Judges on this question that the Courts below ought to have held that the defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land is based upon some misapprehension.

12. As has been indicated above, the learned Judges of the High Court disagreed with the concurrent finding of the two Courts below rejecting the plea of the settlement advanced by the plaintiffs. The plaintiff’s case of separate settlement of each of the two plots of land, appertaining to Khatian No.83 of Mouza Rajarbagh, after their auction purchase by the heirs of Haladhar Dey Sarker, one with Mainuddin by Ext.3 and the other with the plaintiffs by Ext. 3(a) was disbelieved by the learned Subordinate Judge on the grounds that the heir of Haladhar Dey Sarkar did not acquire any right, title and interest in the disputed lands and had, therefore, no authority to settle such land, that the case of surrender of the lands of Khatian No.83 by Maiauddin to the auction purchasers, which was not pleaded but was argued at the time of trial was very improbable and that the settlement by Ext.3 with Mainuddin of only C.S. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre on which a part of his homestead was situated, the remaining part of the homestead, having been upon the other plot, was not acceptable in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the context of these findings the question of genuineness of the rent receipts, Ext. 4 series, which were produced by the plaintiffs in support of their case of settlement of C.S. Plot No.310 with them on the basis of the Kabuliyat, Ext.3(a) was examined by the trial Court as well as by the Court of first appeal who recorded the concurrent finding that those rent receipt were fabricated documents, The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed disagreement with the aforesaid finding on the view that in judging this question the said Court had committed an error in regard to the burden of proof and that, as such, their finding was not tenable in law. We do not think that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in their view that the findings of the Courts below on the question of the genuineness of the rent receipts had been vitiated by a wrong view of the burden of proof and were justified in rejecting the said finding for the purpose of the disposal of the appeal.

13. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have scrutinised each of the thirteen rent receipts which were marked Exts.4-4(k) and noticed the discrepancies and suspicious features in regard to them. He pointed out that either of the two Dakhilas Ext. 4(c) and 4(J) which showed double payment of the rent for the year 1347 BS was fabricated and also expressed the view that Ext 4(k) was spurious and the rent receipts Exts. 4(e) to 4(h) were doubtful, as the alleged payment was made to a person who did not appear to have been appointed as a Tahshilder. The learned Subordinate Judge thereafter considered the question of non-production of the landlord’s collection papers and made the following observation in respect there of:

"Last but not the least, is the fact that though the plaintiffs produced the original Kabuliyat and the sale certificate and certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession taking them from P.W.1. Yet they did not produce the relevant counterfoils of these dakhilas. P.W.1 stated that the counterfoils were very likely with him but he did not bring them. Earlier, he stated that the children of Haladhar Dey Sarkar left 5/7 trunk loads of documents with him. So there is no justifiable ground not to produce the counterfoils.

The production of the counterfoils as well as the other corresponding collection papers were important for another purpose. Not only they would have proved the genuineness of the Dakhilas filed by the plaintiffs and bonafide of their claim of taking settlement of the suit land but it would have also proved that after the auction purchase of the heirs of Haladar Dey Sarkar, Mainuddin paid rent at the rate reserved by the Kabuliyat Ext. 3.............

So the fact that in spite of having 2 able spokesmen on behalf of the heirs of Haladar Dey Sarkar and the custodian of their papers on their side, the plaintiff’s failed to produce the counterfoils of the dakilas file 1 by them and also the other collection papers of the relevant years leads irresistibly to the conclusion that those papers, if produced, would not have supported the plaintiff's case am therefore, unable to place reliance on the dakhilas Ext. 4 series filed by the plaintiffs."

14. The learned Additional District Judge on appeal also examined each of the Dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, and noted the fact of the double payment of the real for the year 1347 B.S. by Ext 4(c) and 4(d), the suspicious character of Ext. 4(k) and ultimately came to the following finding:

"These, I think, lend support to the view that those have been fabricated to bolster up the plaintiff's case and wherever any blank printed form was found it was utilised. Under the circumstances, no reliance can be placed on these dakhilas Exts. 4 series which can be created by stroke of pen at any time and more particularly when it was not supported by counterfoils."

15. It will be found from the findings of the Courts below, as have been quoted above, that on an examination of the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in the light of the circumstances, both of the Courts below arrived at the finding that those Dakhilas were fabricated documents Non-production of counterfoils was found to be circumstance indicating spuriousness of the-said papers. The said findings were not in any way based upon any presumption arising from any burden of proof. The learned Judges of the High Court, however, thought that the said findings had been vitiated by an error committed by the courts below as to the burden of proof applicable to the case. They have proceeded on the view that the Ext. 4 series had been disbelieved by the said Courts only on the ground of non-production of the counterfoils of the said Dakhilas and expressed the view that the primary onus of proving the rent receipts was discharged by the plaintiff as soon as tie rent receipts were produced in the Court from the proper custody and were proved and if the defendants chose to challenge the genuineness of the said Dakhilas, the onus shifted on them to prove their assertion.

The learned Judges expressed their view in the following manner:

"The primary duty to prove these dakhilas for the proof that the Kabuliyat was acted upon is discharged the moment P.W.1 from the landlord's side appeared and admitted these rent receipts. P.W. 1 in the present case a limited that these rent receipts were granted from the shesrista of Haladar Dey Sarkar. When the primary proof of rent receipts have been made, we consider that there is nothing left for the plaintiffs to further adduce evidence by calling for the counterfoils since the landlord accepted the rent receipts granted by them. The burden of proving or otherwise of those rent receipts is shifted on the person who challenges the same."

16. The learned Judges ultimately came to the finding that the plaintiffs having discharged their primary onus of proving the rent receipts, there was no reason why reliance should not be placed on such rent receipts and that the lower appellate Court was not justified in holding that no reliance should be placed on these rent receipts.

<u>17. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to have taken the correct view of the law as to the burden of proof as laid down in the Evidence Act. Section 101 of the Act lays down that whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist and Section 103 of the Act provides that the burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on the person who wishes the Court to believe in its existence unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on the particular person.</u>

<u>18. In this case the plaintiffs have come to the court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext.3 (a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the Dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the Dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a per-son, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the content’s of particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in Section 103B of the Beagal tenancy Act and Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a land-lord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact, on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to pay much attention to the views of the Court below as to the several suspicious features which had been specifically referred to in the judgment of the said Courts but appear to have been influenced in their decision by a wrong view of the law as to the burden of proof. The learned Judges were not correct in the view that the lower appellant court discarded the said rent receipts only on the ground of non-production of counterfoils of the said rent receipts. The question whether a particular rent receipt, proved by a party may, be accepted without the production of the counterfoil of the said rent receipt is a question of fact and depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. Under the circumstances, the learned Judges of the High Court exceeded their jurisdiction wider section 100 of the Act in refusing to accept the concurrent finding of fact of the courts below as to the spurious character of the Dkahilas Ext. 4 series.</u>

19. The finding of the two courts of fact that the plaintiffs were initially inducted upon the disputed land as bargadars under Mainuddin was dependent, to a certain extent, upon their finding on the question of the plaintiff's title, as sought to be established at the trial court by adducing evidence. The plaintiff's case is that the jote of Mani Mohan Dutta, as recorded in Khatian No.82, was auction purchased by the heirs of the decree-holders, Haladar Dey Sarkar, and was thereafter settled with the plaintiffs on 15.1.41 by a Kabuliyat Ext.13(a). The greatest hindrance, found by the Courts below, to the acceptance of the story of settlement as sought to be made out by the plaintiffs, was the character of Mainuddin's interest as recorded in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh and the complete absence of any pleading as to how the said interest was extinguished. Both of the said Courts took the view that the entries in the Khatian clearly showed that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat which was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and, therefore, by the auction sale of the superior right of his landlord, who was a tenure holder his interest as a raiyat was not affected at all. It was pointed out by the trial Court that even if it was held that the interest of Mainuddin was an under raiyati, not protected under section 160 of the Act, it would be an encumbrance which required a notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act for its annulment and that the service of any such notice having not been pleaded nor proved, the interest of Mainuddin could not be extinguished. At the time of the trial a new case as to the surrender by Mainuddin of his interest was sought to be established by proving a Kabuliyat Ext.3. In respect of C.S. plot No.311 and by adducing oral evidence to show that possession of plot No.311 was given up by Mainuddin in favour of the auction purchasers. The story of the surrender of the lands of C.S. Khatian No.83 and the giving up of possession of C.S plot No.310 was completely disbelieved by the said two Courts on an analysis of the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties in respect thereof and on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. One of the points considered by the said Courts in this connection was that the homestead of Mainuddin was not confined to C.S. plot No.311 only but it spread over to a part of C.S. plot No.310 as well.

20. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed to view that the findings of the Courts below that the interest of Mainuddin was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act having been reached without considering the provision contained in section 48G (3) of the Act which lays down that the right of occupancy enjoyed by an under raiyat should not be a protected interest under section 160 of the Act are not tenable in law. This view of the High Court is based upon the assumption that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an under raiyat, but there appears to be absolutely no basis for such an assumption. On a consideration of the entries of the Khatian No.82 and 83 of Mouza Rajarbagb, Ext. 6 and 6(a) both the Courts below came to the view that Mainuddin was a raiyat having a right of occupancy under Mani Mohan Dutta, who was a tenure holder. As a matter of fact, in the said Khatian the superior landlord of Mainuddin was specifically described as "Madhya Swatwadhlkary chiro-sthayee (i.e. parmanent tenure holder) and Mainuddin was stated to be a 'raiyat Sthitiban' i.e. settled raiyat of the village having regard to the said specific description as to Mainuddin being a settled ratyat having a right of occupancy there is hardly any scope for the court to conceive that Mainuddin was an under raiyat.

<u>21. The learned Judges of the High Court seem to have been carried away by the term 'Kole jote’ which was stated to be the interest of Mainuddin in the said khatians, presumably on the assumption that the term 'Jote' invariably indicated the interest of a raiyat. This assumption of the learned Judges is obviously not correct because the term 'Jote' is a general term and sometimes used also to indicate the interest of a tenure holder and it is not necessarily equivalent to a raiyati jote, as was observed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Midnapore Zamindary Co. Vs. Naresb Narayan Singh L.R. 48 I.A. 49. I.L.R.48 Cal. 460 AIR 1922 P.C. 241. Similarly in the case of Krishna Nath Sarker Vs. Uani Kusam Kumar Das, AIR 1923 Cal.351 it was held by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court that the expression 'Jote' was a general term and did not necessarily mean a raiyati and in the facts of that case it was held to be a tenure. On the other hand in the case of Upendra Kishore Sarkar Vs. Sk Khalil, AIR. 1937 Cal. 568: 55 C.LJ, 170 it was held by another Division Bench of the said High Court that the word ‘Jote' might mean even an under raiyati. In the case of Sariatullah Vs. Joinuddin A.I.R 1935 Cal, 463; 39 C.W.N.454. Nasim Ali, J. of the Calcutta high Court in holding that the word 'Jote' did indicate in the facts of that case that it was a tenure made the following observation—</u>

<u>"The plaintiff is described there as Jotedar. The word 'Jote' does not necessarily mean that it is a tenure, Jote simply means a tenancy. Consequently the learned Judge was perfectly justified in looking into the evidence about the user and other circumstances in the case to determine whether the plaintiff's status was that of a tenure holder or a raiyat."</u>

22. Even if the view that the term 'Jote' must neceesarily mean a raiyati Jote and 'Kol-jote' similarly would mean an under raiyat, both the Courts of fact having accepted the status of Mainuddin to be that of a raiyat on the basis of the specific description of such interest to be a raiyati and the jote of the superior landlord as a tenure, the learned Judges of the High Court were not justified in taking the said interest to be an under raiyati without properly coming to a finding that the description of Mainuddin to be a raiat and of his landlord to be a tenure holder in the Khatian was incorrect. The learned Judges of the High Court were not therefore correct in assuming the status of Mani Mohan Dutta the superior landlord of Mainuddin, as that of a raiyat and that of Mainuddin as an under raiyat simply from the description of their interest as Jote and koljote respectively in the C.S Khatian No.83. The term jote is a general expression and means a tenancy and the status of a holder of such a tenancy i.e. whether it is that of a tenure holder or of a raiyat will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. So far as the entries in Khatian No. 83 is concerned the specific nature of the tenancy as described in the terms 'Jote’ and 'Kol jot' were clearly spelt out by the use of expressions Chiro sthayee Madhya Swatwadhikary and sthitiban Raiyat in the Khatian itself, which give rise to statutory presumption as to the correctness of such description. No case as to the incorrectness of these entries in the Khatian was pleaded in the plaint nor any rebutting evidence was adduced by the plaintiffs at the time of the trial, although it was contended at the time of argument that the interest of Mainuddin was not that of raiyat and as such was not protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate-Judge pointed out in his judgment that the term 'Jote' was ambiguous and might mean also tenure and also that it had been admitted by P.W.14, a relation and agent of Haladar Dey Sarkar, the superior landlord of Mani Mohan Dutta, that the status of Mani Mohan Dutta was that of a tenure holder. So the learned Subordinate Judge had no difficulty in coming to the finding that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. On appeal this view was affirmed by the Court of the Additional District Judge. It is significant, as it appears from the judgment of the said Court that no issue was joined on this question on behalf of the plaintiffs and that it was conceded by the learned lawyer appearing on behalf of the appellants in the said appeal that the status of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat. In the Second Appeal, however, this question appears to have been raised by the learned lawyer on behalf of the appellants in spite of their concession on this point in the last court of fact and the learned Judges of the High Court appear to have failed to take notice of the concurrent findings of the Courts below on this question and seem to have been carried away by the expression 'Koljote' as mentioned in the Khatian and assumed that such expression necessarily meant an under raiyati. The learned Judges appear to have held on the basis of such assumption that the provisions of section 48(G) 3 of the Act was attracted and as such the interest of Mainuddin was not a protected interest under section 160 of the Act.

23. It has been pointed out above that there is absolutely no basis for this assumption We have pointed out that the question whether Mainuddin was a raiyat or an under raiyat at is a question of fact and the entries in the C.S. Khatian raised a presumption in favour of the correctness of the entries made in the said khatian. In the absence of any rebutting evidence both the Courts below came to a concurrent finding as to the status of Mainuddin being that of a raiyat, relying upon the said entries and also upon the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case. No error of law or procedure affecting the merits of the case were pointed out in regard to the said finding and as such the said finding was binding upon the High Court in the Second Appeal.

The learned Judges of the High Court clearly exceeded their jurisdiction as conferred by section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure in taking the contrary view as to the status of Mainuddin.

24. The learned Judges, however have taken note of the alternative contention of the defendants that even if the interest of Mainuddin was that of an under raiyat it was an encumbrance which required for its annulment a notice, as prescribed under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, but did not think it necessary to consider the significance of such contention, as it has been stated in the judgment, in view of the defendants case that the plaintiffs were as a matter of fact, put into possession of the disputed land as bargadars, which was not alleged to have been terminated by any forcible dispossession of bargadars. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to have properly appreciated the nature of the plaintiff’s possession of the disputed land as bargadars under the defendants. Such possession is obviously the possession of the defendants who are deemed, in legal parlance to be in constructive possession of the said land through the plaintiffs as their bargadars and the plaintiffs, so long as they were in such possession, were estopped from denying the title of the defendants who had inducted them into such possession. The principle underlying the provision of section 116 of the Evidence Act, read with section 115 of the Act, is clearly applicable to such a case. Although, ordinarily bargadar is not strictly speaking, a tenant nor a licencee, but his position is analogous to either of them. He is a person who is allowed to take possession of some land and cultivate the same, with the permission of a person in possession thereof, on his admitting the latter's authority over the said land. But for this admission he would not certainly have been allowed to get into possession of the said land as a bargadar and as such the law of estoppel is definitely attracted in such a case.

25. The auction purchasers of the interest of Mani Mohan Dutta, even if it was a raiyati, having taken no steps under the law to annul the interest of Mainuddin, even if it was an under raiyati, as an encumbrance, such interest subsisted and if the plaintiffs were inducted upon the disputed land as bargadars in exercise of such interest the possession of the said bargadars was in law possession of the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have missed the legal implication of the plaintiffs possession as bargadars and have therefore observed at one place of their judgment that the definite case of the defendants being that they made barga settlement with the plaintiffs and such case having shown that the plaintiffs were in possession sometime before independence i.e. 14-8-47 and the suit having been filed on 1-3-62 was beyond the statutory period of limitation. The learned Judges seem to be of the view that the plaintiffs possession having admittedly commenced more than 12 years before the institution of the suit, the bar of limitation would be attracted in the case, without noticing that the possession of the plaintiffs as was admitted by the defendants, was in law the possession of defendants them selves.

26. The ultimate finding of the learned Judges of the High Court that the right title and interest of defendants, if any, has been extinguished by adverse possession of the plaintiffs is absolutely a new case which was never pleaded nor sought to be established by means of evidence at the trial. This conclusion of the learned judges of the High Court do not appear to have been reached after properly reversing the concurrent finding of the courts of fact on the question of possession nor does it appear to have been based on an analysis of the evidence on record and the consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. This conclusion appears to have been the result of a misapprehension or misreading of the finding of the said Courts.

27. The learned Judges seem to have rejected the finding of the lower appellate Court on the question of barga settlement of the disputed land with the plaintiffs and defendant’s possession of the said land on the view that the said courts arrived, at a certain stage, at a finding that the defendants failed to prove the barga settlement and also the surrender of the land by the plaintiffs after the expiry of their barga settlement. It has also been observed by the learned Judges in their judgment that, both of the courts below concurrently held that the evidence as to possession on behalf of the plaintiffs were formidable.

<u>28. These were the findings, according to the learned Judges which were arrived at by the lower appellate Court at a certain stage and these findings being contradictory with the final decision of the said Court as to the plaintiffs' entry into the disputed land as bargadars under Mainuddin or his heirs, the said decision, according to the learned Judges was not acceptable. On this view of the matter the learned Judges appear to have rejected the finding of the learned Additional District Judge as totally unacceptable and proceeded straight way to hold that the right, title and interest of the defendants, if any, had been extinguished by the adverse possession of the plaintiffs. It is possible that there may be two findings of a Court which are contradictory with each other and that the contradiction is such that the said findings are irreconcilable with each other.</u>

<u>29. In such a circumstance a Court of Second Appeal may be faced with a paradoxical situation of having two contradictory findings on the same question of fact which cancel each other and in such a situation the second appellate Court may have to remand the case to either of the subordinate courts of fact for a proper finding on the question or may itself review the evidence on record under section 103 of the Code and come to an appropriate finding. The learned Judges do not appear to have followed either of the two courses, which they ought to have done if the view they took of the finding of the Courts below was correct. But instead they appear to proceed to hold straight away, without reference to the pleadings or the evidence on record that the plaintiffs entered into the possession of the disputed land asserting a title hostile to the defendants, the rightful owners, more than 12 years before the institution of the suit and as such the title of the defendants, if any, had been extinguished by adverse possession of the plaintiffs. Such a course is not permissible under law and the aforesaid finding of the learned Judges of the High Courts not, therefore, sustainable</u>.

30. But the learned Judges appear to have made a basic mistake in imagining that the Courts of fact made certain contradictory findings as to the defendant’s failure to prove the barga settlement or surrender of possession by the plaintiffs to the defendants after the expiry of their barga settlement or as to the formidable nature of the evidence as to the plaintiff’s possession. None of the Courts of fact below arrived at any such finding, as suggested in the judgment of the learned Judges of the High Court. What was observed by the learned Additional District Judge is that the direct evidence of barga settlement taken by itself without considering the circumstances, was not satisfactory and that as to the direct oral evidence as regards possession of the disputed land the witnesses were more formidable on the side of the plaintiffs than on the side of the defendants, but that such evidence, if considered along with the circumstances of the case, would be found to have no weight and that it was dangerous to decide the case of the parties on oral evidence alone without considering the circumstance. After considering circumstances of the case and the oral evidence in the light of such circumstances the learned Additional District Judge therefore, came to the following finding:

"If direct oral evidence is weighed on both sides, definitely witnesses are more formidable on the plaintiff’s than the defence. But I think if circumstances have any value than their evidence would not carry any weight. It will be dangerous to decide the case of the parties on oral evidence alone without considering the circumstances, as circumstances cannot lie but witnesses may lie. The fact that the plaintiff took recourse to fabrication of the dakhilas which I had pointed out above would show the way in which the wind was blowing. Had it been bonafide settlement and bonafide possession with regular payment of rent I fail to understand why such fabrication of rent receipts were resorted to. In my opinion taking advantage of the plaintiffs' entry as bargadar they created the Kabuliyat in collusion with the landlord or it might as well be that they created the kabuliyat earlier but knowing that they would not pet possession they by trick of barga entered into possession. Thus considering the case with its attendant circumstances the irresistible conclusion is that the plaintiffs entered into possession of the suit lands as bargadars under Mainuddin or his heirs and as such no question of limitation or adverse possession would come in. I, therefore, find that the plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the suit land that the plaintiffs did not acquire any title by adverse possession."

31. No error of law or procedure could be pointed out in respect of the findings of the Court below referred to above, and as such none of the conclusions of the learned Judges of the High Court contrary to the said finding are sustainable in law.

The result, therefore, is that the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment and decree of the High Court it set aside and those of the Courts below are restored.

End.
